20261118-physics-g03.s.s1.prompt: [G03 Physics Inquiry] On a frictionless horizontal surface, a constant horizontal force of $F = 10\text{ N}$ is applied to an object of mass $m = 2\text{ kg}$, moving it $4\text{ m}$. Which of the following statements about the work $W$ done on the object and its acceleration $a$ is correct?
20261118-physics-g03.s.s1.explain:
Step 1: By Newton's second law $F = ma$, $a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{10\text{ N}}{2\text{ kg}} = 5\text{ m/s}^2$.
Step 2: The amount of work done is $W = F \cdot s = 10\text{ N} \times 4\text{ m} = 40\text{ J}$.
Step 3: Therefore, the acceleration is $5\text{ m/s}^2$ and the work done is $40\text{ J}$.

20261118-physics-g03.s.s1.hint.1: Definition of work: Use the formula $W = F \times s$.

20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.prompt: [G03 Physics Inquiry (Advanced·Applied)] Near Earth's surface, an object of mass $m = 1\text{ kg}$ is dropped from rest at a height of $h = 20\text{ m}$ in free fall. (Take $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ and neglect air resistance.) Which statement regarding the conservation of mechanical energy and the speed $v$ just before hitting the ground is correct?
20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.explain:
Step 1: Neglecting air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved throughout the fall.
Step 2: Potential energy at the top converts to kinetic energy at the ground: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Step 3: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 \times 20\text{ m}} = \sqrt{392} \approx 19.8\text{ m/s}$.
20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.hint.0: Ignoring air resistance, the law of conservation of mechanical energy holds: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.o.o0: Mechanical energy is conserved, and the speed just before reaching the ground is approximately $19.8\text{ m/s}$.
20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.o.o1: Mechanical energy decreases during the fall, and the speed just before reaching the ground is approximately $9.8\text{ m/s}$.
20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.o.o2: Only potential energy is conserved, and kinetic energy becomes 0.
20261121-physics-g03-2.s.s1.o.o3: Gravitational acceleration increases over time, so speed cannot be calculated.

20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.prompt: [G04 Physics Inquiry (Advanced·Applied)] Near Earth's surface, an object of mass $m = 1\text{ kg}$ is dropped from rest at a height of $h = 20\text{ m}$ in free fall. (Take $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ and neglect air resistance.) Which statement regarding the conservation of mechanical energy and the speed $v$ just before hitting the ground is correct?
20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.explain:
Step 1: Neglecting air resistance, mechanical energy is conserved throughout the fall.
Step 2: Potential energy at the top converts to kinetic energy at the ground: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
Step 3: $v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 \times 20\text{ m}} = \sqrt{392} \approx 19.8\text{ m/s}$.
20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.hint.0: Ignoring air resistance, the law of conservation of mechanical energy holds: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.o.o0: Mechanical energy is conserved, and the speed just before reaching the ground is approximately $19.8\text{ m/s}$.
20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.o.o1: Mechanical energy decreases during the fall, and the speed just before reaching the ground is approximately $9.8\text{ m/s}$.
20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.o.o2: Only potential energy is conserved, and kinetic energy becomes 0.
20261121-physics-g04-2.s.s1.o.o3: Gravitational acceleration increases over time, so speed cannot be calculated.
